title: Hybrid SD-WAN Onramp and E2E DNS Resolution Notes
body:
Purpose:
This note collects experiment results and decisions from the customer POC for hybrid SD-WAN onramp into Redwood Private deployments. Focus: how to achieve consistent egress behavior, deterministic DNS resolution (split-horizon), and minimal customer firewall changes for regulated customers with existing SD-WAN / MPLS backbones.

Context / customer constraints:
- Customer runs SD-WAN at branch offices with local internet breakouts configured by policy (company-managed).
- Security team prefers egress anchoring in cloud for audit, TLS inspection, and outbound allowlisting (they want to control destination IPs).
- Minimal changes allowed at branch firewalls (no per-route BGP exchanges with Redwood).
- Need low-latency path for interactive chat features; tolerate small increases in RTT for batch embedding workloads.

Design options considered (short):
1) Hairpin egress (preferred for POC): branch -> SD-WAN hub -> customer transit -> cloud egress (NAT at customer transit/VPC) -> Redwood private endpoint. Pros: keeps control in customer network, minimal per-branch config. Cons: longer path, double NAT, DNS split-horizon complexity.
2) Direct branch-to-cloud with static NAT (branch IGW rules permit specific Redwood IPs): Pros: lower latency for branches with public breakouts. Cons: must manage allowlists at many branch firewalls.
3) BGP over VPN to Redwood (peering): Pros: clean routing and direct prefixes. Cons: operationally heavy, not allowed by customer.

Decision (POC): implement hairpin egress via customer-managed transit VPC peering + split-horizon DNS anchored at transit. Evaluate latency and DNS correctness; fallback to static-allowlist plan for high-volume branches.

DNS resolution approach (E2E):
Goal: requests from branch endpoints must resolve Redwood private endpoints to transit/VPC-private IPs so response path stays inside customer's network where required.
Implementation plan:
- Create a split-horizon DNS zone in customer's DNS (Route53/on-prem): internal zone returns transit IPs for service.redwood.private. External resolves to public ingress.
- At the transit VPC, run an outbound-forwarder (Unbound/Bind) that forwards any unknown names to Redwood's private DNS proxy over the secure peering link (TLS/mTLS).
- Ensure EDNS-client-subnet is disabled between forwarders to prevent leakage of branch IPs to upstream.
- TTL strategy: use short TTL (30s-60s) for onramp VIPs to support quick failover during canary rollouts.

Sample DNS flow (branch client):
1) client -> local resolver (SD-WAN local DNS cache).
2) local resolver queries internal split-horizon zone - returns transit IP for service.redwood.private.
3) client connects to transit IP; transit NATs to Redwood Private endpoint (src preserved where possible for auditing).

Networking / NAT considerations:
- NAT44 double-NAT risk: branch NAT -> transit NAT -> Redwood NAT. We recommend preserving source where possible by using 1:1 NAT at the transit (SNAT only when egressing to public). For inbound auditing to Redwood, include X-Forwarded-For or embed customer metadata in mutual TLS SNI (subjectAltName) if supported.
- Keep MTU in mind: SD-WAN overlays reduce effective MTU; enable MSS clamping on the egress proxy and ensure the inference MTU >= 1350 to avoid fragmentation with long requests.

Security controls and allowlisting:
- Customer wants a small set of destination IPs for external allowlists. For the hairpin approach, publish transit egress IPs (these are customer-managed) to their security teams.
- For Redwood side, we will provide a validated certificate bundle and expected SNI values instead of IPs when possible to reduce churn.
- Mutual TLS for control-plane DNS and health checks (mTLS between transit forwarder and Redwood DNS proxy).

Health checks and observability:
- Active probes from transit into Redwood private endpoint on 443 and a health path (/healthz) every 10s. Alert on 5-minute consecutive failures.
- Redwood will expose per-route latency and error metrics to the customer's monitoring integration (Prometheus push / CloudWatch).
- Tracing: include a hop header (X-RW-Onramp: <transit-id>) so Redwood logs can attribute requests per-transit.

Performance testing plan (POC tasks):
- Latency microbench: run 500 samples of 1-token completion and compare branch->Redwood via hairpin vs direct public path (if available). Target: hairpin < +15ms median increase relative to direct public path.
- Throughput: validate batching at Redwood for embeddings from branch; target no more than 10% throughput loss.
- DNS correctness: simulate zonal failover (update split-horizon) and confirm client re-resolves within TTL window.

Configuration snippets (examples):
- iptables (transit NAT):
  iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -s 10.0.0.0/16 -d <redwood_private_prefix> -j SNAT --to-source <transit-egress-ip>

- Unbound minimal forwarder conf (transit):
  forward-zone:
    name: "service.redwood.private"
    forward-addr: 10.200.10.12@853  # Redwood DNS proxy (mTLS)

- Example healthcheck curl:
  curl -v --resolve service.redwood.private:443:10.200.20.5 https://service.redwood.private/healthz

Operational checklist for POC run:
- [ ] Confirm transit has stable IPs and publish to customer security for allowlist (if needed).
- [ ] Deploy split-horizon zone and test A/AAAA records for service.redwood.private.
- [ ] Deploy Unbound forwarder + mTLS certs to transit; verify TLS handshake to Redwood DNS proxy.
- [ ] Run synthetic latency and throughput tests from 3 representative branches (US-east, EU-west, APAC).
- [ ] Validate metrics ingestion into customer's dashboard and set baseline alerts.
- [ ] Record rollback steps (switch split-horizon back to public, remove NAT rule).

Open questions / risks:
- Will the customer's security team accept heading-based metadata in logs instead of preserving true source IP? If not, we must support an IP-preserving transit NAT (requires extra routing work).
- SD-WAN vendor behavior on DNS caching: some vendors will ignore TTLs for performance; need to identify vendors and test TTL behavior early.
- Certificate rotation for transit mTLS: define automation cadence and CRON jobs to rotate.

Next steps (owner and ETA):
- Sofia: validate Unbound-forwarder config with customer infra (ETA 2024-03-12).
- Liam: run latency microbenchmark from EU test branch (ETA 2024-03-08).
- Priya: coordinate security allowlist workshop with customer (ETA 2024-03-15).

Appendix - ASCII diagram:

  Branch Client (10.10.1.0/24)
       |
    SD-WAN Local Breakout (policy)
       |
    -- overlay --> SD-WAN Hub / Edge
       | (internal route to)
  Customer Transit VPC (10.200.0.0/16)  -- NAT / split-horizon DNS & forwarder -->  Redwood Private Endpoint (10.200.20.5)

Notes from troubleshooting sessions:
- Observed stale DNS answers from SD-WAN cache: increased Unbound TTL and forced cache flush on hub reduced incidents.
- Initial MSS-related fragmentation causing gRPC failures; resolved with MSS clamp to 1350 at the transit edge.
